name: Tap water / fluoride avoidance

lead: Some appearance-focused people avoid tap water to avoid fluoride, and sometimes chlorine, presenting it as part of a skin and health routine. Health bodies such as the WHO and CDC support fluoridation at recommended levels, while critics dispute its benefit and safety.
Fluoride is added to public water to reduce tooth decay, with a US recommended level of 0.7 mg/L. No study has tested whether avoiding fluoride changes how someone looks.

paras: People use home filters, bottled or spring water for drinking and cooking, and sometimes shower filters for washing. It is a permanent household switch rather than a short course.

Fluoridation's documented adverse effect at recommended levels is mostly mild dental fluorosis. Neurodevelopment concerns are debated, and a 2024 US court ruling addressed IQ risk. Reduced fluoride exposure is associated with more cavities in some reviews.

angle.text: Some appearance-focused users drink and wash with filtered or spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, aiming for healthier skin and teeth. Health bodies back fluoridation, critics dispute it, and no study has looked at appearance.

lead: Tap water / fluoride avoidance is a lifestyle practice in which people drink and sometimes wash with filtered, bottled or spring water instead of municipal tap water, mainly to avoid fluoride, and sometimes chlorine. In appearance-focused communities it is presented as part of a health-and-skin routine.

Water fluoridation is the controlled addition of fluoride to public water supplies to reduce tooth decay; the US recommended level is 0.7 mg/L.[1] Health bodies including the WHO, the FDI World Dental Federation and the US CDC endorse it as safe and effective at recommended levels, while opponents argue the benefit is small and that safety is uncertain.[1][2] No published study was found that tests fluoride avoidance for facial appearance.

paras: Fluoride is added to public water mainly as sodium fluoride, fluorosilicic acid or sodium fluorosilicate; it does not change the water's taste, smell or look.[1] Grand Rapids, Michigan, began fluoridating on January 25, 1945, the first city to do so, after decades of research into the staining of teeth in areas with naturally fluoride-rich water.[1]

Some countries and cities, including Finland, Germany, Japan, the Netherlands and Switzerland, do not fluoridate or have stopped; Basel, for example, uses fluoridated salt.[1] Israel dropped mandatory fluoridation in 2014.[1][2]

sections.h: Positions of health bodies and critics
paras: The WHO, FDI and US CDC endorse fluoridation, and the CDC named it one of the ten great public health achievements of the 20th century in 1999.[1][2] A 2015 Cochrane review estimated 35% fewer cavities in baby teeth and 26% in permanent teeth in children, but rated the evidence as poor and found no conclusive adult research.[1][2]

The 2011 European Commission review saw no clear advantage over topical fluoride, and the 2007 Nuffield Council on Bioethics found good evidence for or against lacking.[1][2] Opponents raise consent, cost-effectiveness, precaution and conflict-of-interest arguments.[2] In September 2024 a US federal judge ruled in Food and Water Watch v. EPA that fluoridation posed an unreasonable risk of reduced IQ in children, requiring an EPA regulatory response.[2]

Dental fluorosis is the only clear adverse effect at recommended levels; Cochrane estimated about 12% of people at 0.7 ppm had fluorosis of aesthetic concern, mostly mild.[1] Little effect on fracture risk and no clear link to cancer has been reported, and rare acute poisonings have followed improper dosing, including a fatal 1992 Alaska outbreak.[1]
Practitioners cite avoiding fluoride and chlorine as a reason for filtered or spring water. See Filtered / spring water. Published sources reviewed here do not discuss fluoride and facial appearance.
No studies found on fluoride avoidance and facial appearance. Studies of water fluoridation concern dental and general health outcomes, summarised above.[1][2]

timeline.event: Grand Rapids, Michigan begins fluoridating its water.[1]
WHO sets a 1.5 mg/L guideline maximum.[2]
Cochrane review of fluoridation in children.[1][2]
US federal court ruling in Food and Water Watch v. EPA.[2]
